title: Sizing and Loss-Adjusted Performance Assessment of Chilled-Water Thermal Energy Storage for Peak Load Shaving in a Large-Scale Automotive Manufacturing Facility in Saudi Arabia
content: Thermal Energy Storage (TES) is increasingly relevant for large industrial facilities operating in hot climates, where cooling demand coincides with high electrical peak periods. Although TES has been widely discussed in commercial buildings and district cooling systems, fewer published case studies quantify its integrated technical, financial, and environmental value in large-scale automotive manufacturing environments, and fewer still demonstrate a reproducible optimization basis for the selected TES size. This paper addresses that gap through a design-stage techno-economic case study -- not yet validated against field-measured operating data -- of a large-scale automotive manufacturing facility in Saudi Arabia, where a chilled-water TES system was sized using a closed-form capacity-minimization model and integrated with the central utility plant and Building Management System (BMS). The system uses a partial-storage strategy in which a 71,500 TR-hr chilled-water TES tank (usable capacity; physical tank sized to 85,800 TR-hr gross, including a 20% operating margin for state-of-charge limits, thermocline management, control tolerance, and design contingency, Section 5.1) is charged during off-peak hours and discharged during daytime peak hours. The TES is integrated with a central utility plant of six water-cooled centrifugal chillers rated at 3,000 TR each, arranged as five duty units and one standby unit in the baseline configuration.The design-stage model shows that the TES strategy reduces the required peak chiller plant output by 4,353 TR (29.0% of the 15,000 TR baseline) -- the paper's most robust and directly verifiable result. This figure incorporates the project-design TES round-trip efficiency of 0.85; the 6C design temperature differential is used separately to determine storage volume (Section 4.2), not in this capacity calculation. Because charging the tank at night to make up for round-trip losses requires more chiller output than the tank later delivers during the day, the required capacity is governed by the nighttime charging regime rather than the daytime discharge regime (Section 4.2). Because the case-study chillers are available only in discrete 3,000 TR increments and the facility requires N+1 standby redundancy, the implementable equipment configuration for the TES-assisted case is 4 duty units (12,000 TR nameplate) plus 1 standby unit, compared with 5 duty units plus 1 standby in the baseline -- one fewer physical chiller. Evaluated against this discrete configuration, reported project outcomes are approximately USD 2.41 million in net CAPEX saving; a bottom-up-verified electricity-cost saving of approximately USD 43,805/year, alongside a broader illustrative upper-bound OPEX scenario of up to approximately USD 2.10 million/year (including non-itemized maintenance and water-treatment allowances) pending facility-level verification (Section 6.1); a net annual electricity saving of approximately 0.82 million kWh (1.6%); and an estimated annual Scope 2 emissions reduction of approximately 568 tCO2/year associated with the modeled net electricity saving. These economic and energy benefits are substantially smaller than the peak-capacity result because operating only 4 chillers at up to 88.7% average loading during the nighttime charging period -- above the 80% per-unit staging threshold used elsewhere in this model -- is measurably less efficient than the 5-chiller, lower-loading operation implied by a continuous (non-discretized) capacity model. A closed-form optimization, assuming lossless charge/discharge cycling, shows that the selected 71,500 TR-hr TES size is the capacity that minimizes required chiller capacity across the full daily cycle; incorporating the project-design round-trip efficiency shows the loss-adjusted optimum is somewhat smaller, near 65,300 TR-hr (Section 4.2). The adopted 71,500 TR-hr capacity is retained because it reflects the facility's actual project design, not because it is the mathematical optimum under the complete loss-adjusted, discrete-equipment model. Peak-capacity reduction, annual energy-consumption reduction, and net CAPEX benefit are related but distinct objectives that are not maximized by the same TES size or the same equipment configuration. The case demonstrates that a large industrial chilled-water TES system can substantially reduce required peak chiller capacity, but that the magnitude of the resulting energy, economic, and environmental benefit depends strongly on TES losses, discrete equipment configuration, and auxiliary pumping.
